analogy.p: Think of squash (cordial) in a glass of water. Putting two spoonfuls of squash into a small glass gives a strong-tasting, concentrated drink; putting the same two spoonfuls into a jug of water gives a dilute drink. The amount of squash (solute) is the same, but it is spread through more water, so the concentration is lower. The analogy breaks down because squash is a mixture of many things and its 'strength' is a matter of taste, whereas in chemistry concentration is an exact measurement (g or mol per dm³) and strength has a separate meaning related to ionisation.

bullets: **Solute** + **solvent** = **solution**; in an aqueous solution the solvent is water.
Concentration = amount of solute ÷ volume of solution; it compares *how much* with *how big*.
The AQA specification measures concentration as a **mass per given volume**, e.g. **grams per dm³ (g/dm³)**.
At Higher tier you also use **moles per dm³ (mol/dm³)**, which counts particles rather than grams.
Two solutions can contain the same mass of solute but have different concentrations if their volumes differ.
Concentrated and dilute describe the *relative* amount of solute, not how strong or weak an acid is.
Link: concentration controls rate of reaction and is used in titrations to find unknown concentrations.
core.p: Many chemical reactions happen in **solution**, which is a **solute** (the substance that dissolves) mixed completely into a **solvent** (usually water). The **concentration** of a solution tells you **how much solute is dissolved in a given volume of solution**. A solution with a lot of solute in each unit of volume is **concentrated**; one with only a little is **dilute**. Concentration matters because the amount of reacting particles in a given volume controls how fast a reaction happens and how much product can form from a measured volume.

bullets: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1 litre; 1 cm³ = 0.001 dm³ (also equal to 1 millilitre, ml).
Convert volume in cm³ to dm³ **before** substituting into the equation.
Writing the conversion line (‘25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0250 dm³’) earns a method mark.
The symbol for a litre is not used on the AQA papers; use dm³.
A common error is dividing by 100 instead of 1000.
Check: a typical conical flask holds 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³.
core.h: Units of volume: cm³ and dm³
core.p: Concentration questions often fail because of unit errors. The **decimetre cubed (dm³)** is the same as a **litre**, and **1 dm³ = 1000 cm³**. Laboratory glassware (measuring cylinders, pipettes, burettes) is usually marked in **cm³**, but concentration is normally given **per dm³**, so you must convert. To convert **cm³ to dm³ divide by 1000**; to convert **dm³ to cm³ multiply by 1000**. Do this conversion **first**, before using any formula.

bullets: Concentration (g/dm³) = mass of solute (g) ÷ volume (dm³).
Mass of solute (g) = concentration (g/dm³) × volume (dm³).
Volume (dm³) = mass (g) ÷ concentration (g/dm³).
Example: 5.0 g of NaCl in 250 cm³: 5.0 ÷ 0.250 = **20 g/dm³**.
Example: 0.40 mol would be a different unit; do not mix g/dm³ and mol/dm³ in one calculation.
Use a formula triangle (mass at the top; concentration and volume at the bottom) if it helps, but always write the rearranged formula.
Give the answer with units g/dm³ and to the same significant figures as the data.
core.h: Concentration in g/dm³: the equation and rearrangements
core.p: The first way to express concentration is as a **mass of solute per volume of solution**. The equation is **concentration (g/dm³) = mass of solute (g) ÷ volume of solution (dm³)**. Rearranging gives **mass (g) = concentration (g/dm³) × volume (dm³)** and **volume (dm³) = mass (g) ÷ concentration (g/dm³)**. The units tell you the operation: 'grams per dm³' means grams divided by dm³. A concentration of 20 g/dm³ means every 1 dm³ of solution contains 20 g of the solute.

bullets: Step 1: convert cm³ to dm³ (÷ 1000).
Step 2: mass = concentration × volume.
150 cm³ of 20 g/dm³ NaCl: 20 × 0.150 = 3.0 g.
Doubling the volume doubles the mass; doubling the concentration also doubles the mass.
Check the answer is sensible: a small volume (cm³) of solution should contain a small mass of solute.
To find how much solution holds 4.0 g at 20 g/dm³: 4.0 ÷ 20 = 0.20 dm³ = 200 cm³.
core.h: Calculating the mass of solute in a given volume
core.p: The AQA specification specifically asks you to **calculate the mass of solute in a given volume of solution of known concentration**. The method has two steps: **convert the volume to dm³**, then **multiply by the concentration**. For example, a solution of copper sulfate has a concentration of 40 g/dm³. The mass of solute in 50 cm³ is 40 × (50 ÷ 1000) = 40 × 0.050 = **2.0 g**. You can also find how much solution contains a required mass by rearranging: volume = mass ÷ concentration.

bullets: Weigh the solute using a **balance** (e.g. to 0.01 g) and record the mass.
Dissolve in a beaker with a little distilled water, stirring with a glass rod.
Pour into the **volumetric flask**, using a funnel, and rinse the beaker and rod into the flask.
Fill with distilled water until the **bottom of the meniscus** is on the line, adding the last drops with a dropping pipette.
Stopper and invert several times to make the solution **uniform**.
Distilled (not tap) water is used because tap water contains dissolved ions.
Accuracy depends on weighing precisely, transferring all the solute and reading the meniscus at eye level.
core.h: Making a solution of known concentration (practical skills)
core.p: To make a solution of a known concentration you must **weigh the solute accurately, dissolve it fully and make the total volume up exactly**. First weigh the solid on a **balance** in a weighing boat (or beaker). Dissolve it in **less than the final volume** of distilled water in a beaker, stirring until no solid remains. Transfer the solution to a **volumetric flask**, rinsing the beaker into the flask so none of the solute is lost, then add **distilled water until the bottom of the meniscus touches the graduation mark**. Stopper the flask and invert it to mix. This gives a solution of precisely known concentration.

bullets: More solute particles per unit volume = higher concentration.
On dilution, the **moles of solute remain constant**: moles before = moles after.
Dilution factor: new concentration = old concentration × (old volume ÷ new volume).
Example: 100 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ made up to 500 cm³ gives 2.0 × 100 ÷ 500 = **0.40 mol/dm³**.
Adding water to a solution does not change the mass of solute; it changes the volume.
Concentrated solutions have a higher rate of reaction because collisions are more frequent.
'Concentrated' and 'dilute' are not the same as 'strong' and 'weak' for acids (see strength vs concentration).
core.p: On a particle level, a **concentrated** solution has **many solute particles in each unit of volume**, while a **dilute** solution has **fewer solute particles in the same volume**. When you **dilute** a solution by adding water, the **amount (moles) and mass of solute stay exactly the same**, but they are spread through a larger volume, so the concentration falls. This explains why a more concentrated acid reacts faster: more particles per cm³ mean more frequent collisions between reacting particles.

bullets: Concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³).
Moles = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³).
Volume (dm³) = moles ÷ concentration.
Example: 25.0 cm³ of 0.50 mol/dm³ NaOH: moles = 0.50 × 0.0250 = **0.0125 mol**.
Example: mass of NaOH needed for 250 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³: moles = 0.10 × 0.250 = 0.025 mol; mass = 0.025 × 40 = **1.0 g**.
Symbol notation: [HCl] means concentration of HCl, but you can write 'concentration of HCl' in words.
Always convert cm³ to dm³ first.
core.p: At Higher tier, concentration can be expressed as the **amount of solute in moles per dm³ of solution**. The equation is **concentration (mol/dm³) = amount of solute (mol) ÷ volume (dm³)**, which rearranges to **moles = concentration × volume (in dm³)** and **volume = moles ÷ concentration**. This is more useful than g/dm³ in reaction calculations because balanced equations give mole ratios. A **1.0 mol/dm³** solution contains 1 mole (6.02 × 10²³ particles) of solute in every dm³ of solution.

bullets: g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr.
mol/dm³ = g/dm³ ÷ Mr.
Example: 4.0 g/dm³ NaOH (Mr 40) = 4.0 ÷ 40 = **0.10 mol/dm³**.
Sulfuric acid: Mr = 98; 0.125 mol/dm³ = 12.25 g/dm³ (12 g/dm³ to 2 s.f.).
Alternative path: convert g to moles first (÷ Mr), then divide by volume in dm³.
Write the Mr calculation clearly to secure the method mark.
core.h: Converting between g/dm³ and mol/dm³ (Higher tier)
core.p: The two measures of concentration are linked by the **relative formula mass**. To go from **mol/dm³ to g/dm³, multiply by Mr**; to go from **g/dm³ to mol/dm³, divide by Mr**. This works because 1 mole of a substance has a mass of Mr grams, so 1 dm³ of a 1 mol/dm³ solution contains Mr grams. Converting is essential when a question gives a concentration in one unit but asks for another or when you need the moles of a solution given in g/dm³.

bullets: Step 1: write the balanced equation.
Step 2: moles of the solution whose concentration and volume you know = conc × volume (dm³).
Step 3: use the ratio to find the moles of the other reactant.
Step 4: unknown concentration = moles ÷ volume (dm³), or volume = moles ÷ concentration.
Step 5: convert to g/dm³ by multiplying by Mr if the question asks for it.
Remember 1 : 2 ratios, e.g. H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O, where acid moles are half the alkali moles.
Keep extra digits in the working and round only at the end.
core.h: Using concentration and volume with equation ratios (Higher tier)
core.p: Most exam questions combine concentration with a balanced equation. The pattern is: **moles of known = concentration × volume (dm³)**, then use the **balancing numbers** to find **moles of the other substance**, then convert to the quantity asked for (concentration, volume or mass). This is the same ratio method as for reacting masses, but the starting moles come from concentration × volume rather than mass ÷ Mr.

bullets: Rinse the pipette with the solution it will measure, and the burette with the solution it will contain, to avoid dilution.
Use a **pipette filler** (never mouth-pipette) to place 25.0 cm³ of the solution in a clean conical flask.
Add 2-3 drops of indicator: **methyl orange** (red in acid, yellow in alkali) or **phenolphthalein** (colourless in acid, pink in alkali).
Fill the burette, remove the funnel, and record the starting volume at eye level, reading the **bottom of the meniscus**.
Swirl the flask continuously on a **white tile** so the colour change is easy to see.
Near the end-point add the solution **drop by drop** until a single drop changes the colour permanently.
Calculate the **mean titre** from the **concordant** results only (within 0.10 cm³); ignore the rough titration and any outlier.
core.h: Required practical: titration (chemistry only / Higher application)
core.p: A **titration** finds the **exact volume of one solution that reacts completely with a known volume of another**. A **pipette** measures a fixed volume (usually 25.0 cm³) of one solution (often the alkali) into a **conical flask**, and a few drops of **indicator** are added. The other solution (often the acid) is added from a **burette** until the indicator **just changes colour**: the **end-point**. Reading the burette before and after gives the **titre**. A first **rough titration** finds the approximate end-point, then you repeat carefully, adding **dropwise** near the end-point, until you have **concordant results** (usually within 0.10 cm³).

bullets: Example: 25.0 cm³ NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ HCl; NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O (1 : 1).
Moles HCl = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol; moles NaOH = 0.00200 mol.
Concentration of NaOH = 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = **0.0800 mol/dm³**.
For a 1 : 2 equation, e.g. H2SO4 + 2NaOH, halve or double the moles accordingly.
Mean titre from concordant results = (sum of concordant titres) ÷ number of concordant titres.
State the answer with units and sensible significant figures (usually 3 s.f. here).
core.h: Titration calculation step by step (Higher tier)
core.p: To calculate an unknown concentration from a titration, apply the mole method to the titre. First write the **balanced equation**. Then calculate the **moles of the solution for which you know the concentration and volume** (concentration × volume in dm³). Use the **equation ratio** to find the moles of the other reactant, then divide by its volume (the pipette volume) to find its **concentration in mol/dm³**. If asked, convert to **g/dm³** by multiplying by Mr. Using this routine reduces mistakes with ratios and units.

bullets: Read the meniscus at eye level; reading from above or below gives parallax error.
Always remove the funnel from the burette before reading, because drips falling from it change the volume.
Rinsing the conical flask with distilled water does not matter, but rinsing with the solution would add extra moles.
Using a pipette instead of a measuring cylinder increases the accuracy of the volume of the solution in the flask.
Dropwise addition near the end-point reduces the chance of overshooting.
Concordant titres show that the results are repeatable.
Using a white tile and the same person to judge the colour change reduces end-point judgement error.
core.h: Sources of error and improving accuracy
core.p: The accuracy of concentration measurements depends on careful technique and on the **resolution** of the equipment. A burette reads to 0.05 cm³, a pipette is more precise than a measuring cylinder, and a volumetric flask gives a more precise volume than a beaker. **Random errors** (e.g. misjudging the end-point) are reduced by repeating and calculating a mean; **systematic errors** (e.g. the burette not rinsed, or a balance that always reads high) shift all results the same way and are removed by correcting the technique or equipment. A repeat that agrees closely shows that the results are **precise** and **repeatable**.

bullets: Strong acid: completely ionised in solution (HCl, H2SO4, HNO3); weak acid: partially ionised (ethanoic, citric, carbonic).
Concentration describes how many moles/grams per dm³; strength describes the degree of ionisation.
Increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution **increases the rate** because there are more particles per unit volume, so more frequent successful collisions.
For each ×10 increase in hydrogen ion concentration, the pH falls by 1 unit (Higher tier).
Titration results link to **neutralisation** and **salt preparation**.
Concentration appears in **electrolysis** of solutions and in **equilibrium** (changing concentration shifts equilibrium).
Use moles ÷ volume for gases only in the form of volume = moles × 24 dm³ at RTP.
core.h: Concentration vs strength, rates and other links
core.p: Be careful to distinguish **concentration** from **strength**. **Concentration** is the amount of acid or alkali dissolved in a given volume. **Strength** (of acids) describes **how much the acid ionises (dissociates) in water**. A strong acid such as HCl is almost completely ionised; a weak acid such as ethanoic acid is only partly ionised. You can have a **dilute strong acid** or a **concentrated weak acid**. Concentration also links to **rate of reaction** (higher concentration means more frequent collisions), to **pH** (a tenfold increase in H⁺ concentration lowers the pH by one), and to **percentage yield and gas calculations**.

exam: Command words: **calculate** (show every step with units), **describe** (give the method in order), **explain** (give reasons using ideas such as particles per unit volume), **suggest** (apply your knowledge to a new context).
1-mark questions: convert 250 cm³ to dm³, state the unit of concentration, or name the apparatus (burette, pipette, volumetric flask).
2-mark calculations: concentration = mass ÷ volume, with a mark for the conversion to dm³ and one for the answer.
3-4 mark calculations (Higher): moles = conc × volume; use the ratio; find the unknown concentration; convert to g/dm³ with Mr.
Model phrase for dilution: 'the same number of moles of solute is now in a larger volume, so the concentration decreases'.
Model phrase for rate: 'a higher concentration means more particles per unit volume so more frequent collisions, so a faster rate'.
For the titration method: mention rinsing, pipette, indicator, dropwise at the end-point, swirling, white tile and repeating until concordant.
Describe concordant results as 'within 0.10 cm³ of each other' and say that you use them to calculate the mean titre.
6-mark practical question: plan the order (prepare apparatus, rough run, accurate runs, concordant, mean), include safety (eye protection, spills) and accuracy points.
Data questions: calculate the mean titre only from concordant values and show the sum and division.
Always give units (g/dm³ or mol/dm³) and a sensible number of significant figures.

mistakes.w: Using volume in cm³ in the formula (e.g. 20 ÷ 250).
Dividing by 100 instead of 1000 when converting cm³ to dm³.

mistakes.r: Concentration is amount per dm³; strength is how much the acid ionises; they are independent.
mistakes.w: Saying a concentrated acid is the same as a strong acid.

mistakes.r: Dilution adds solvent; the mass and moles of solute stay the same, so the concentration falls.
Convert using Mr (g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr) so that units are consistent.
mistakes.w: Mixing g/dm³ and mol/dm³ in one equation.

mistakes.r: Calculate the mean only from concordant titres, within 0.10 cm³.
mistakes.w: Including the rough titration (or an outlier) in the mean titre.

mistakes.r: Use the balancing numbers: 1 mol H2SO4 neutralises 2 mol NaOH.
mistakes.w: Ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio in a titration equation (e.g. H2SO4 with NaOH).

mistakes.r: Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
mistakes.w: Reading the burette at the top of the meniscus or from above.

mistakes.r: Rinse with the solution it will hold so that it is not diluted.
mistakes.w: Rinsing the burette or pipette with water only.

summary: You must be able to calculate the concentration of a solution in g/dm³, find the mass of solute in a given volume of known concentration, and at Higher tier use mol/dm³ and titration data with balanced equations. This matters because almost every reaction in a lab or industry uses solutions, and concentration controls both how much product forms and how fast.

terms.d: The substance that dissolves in a solvent to make a solution.
The liquid in which a solute dissolves, e.g. water.
A mixture formed when a solute dissolves completely in a solvent.
A solution in which the solvent is water, shown by the state symbol (aq).
The amount of solute in a given volume of solution, e.g. g/dm³ or mol/dm³.
A solution containing a large amount of solute in a given volume.
A solution containing a small amount of solute in a given volume.
Cubic decimetre; equal to 1000 cm³ or one litre.
The unit of amount of substance; 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
A method for finding the volume of one solution that reacts exactly with a known volume of another.
A long graduated tube with a tap used to add a variable, measured volume of liquid in a titration.
Apparatus used to measure a fixed volume of liquid accurately, e.g. 25.0 cm³.
A substance that changes colour to show the end-point of a reaction, e.g. in a titration.
The point in a titration at which the indicator changes colour, showing the reaction is just complete.
Titration results that are close together, usually within 0.10 cm³.
The volume of solution added from the burette to reach the end-point.
A flask with a single graduation mark used to make up a precise volume of solution.

worked.q: A student dissolves 5.0 g of sodium chloride in water to make 250 cm³ of solution. (a) Calculate the concentration in g/dm³. (b) Calculate the mass of sodium chloride in 150 cm³ of this solution. [4 marks]

25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O. Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide in (a) mol/dm³ and (b) g/dm³. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1) [5 marks, Higher tier]

25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid: H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O. Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid in g/dm³. (Mr H2SO4 = 98) [5 marks, Higher tier]
steps: Ratio 2 NaOH : 1 H2SO4, so moles H2SO4 = 0.00500 ÷ 2 = 0.00250 mol.
